title: Cleobis and Biton Pull Their Mother's Cart
text:
Herodotus tells how Solon, the wise lawgiver of Athens, visited Croesus, the fabulously rich king of Lydia. Croesus showed him his treasures and asked who was the happiest man Solon had ever seen, expecting to hear his own name. Solon first named an Athenian, Tellus, who had lived well and died bravely for his city. Croesus then asked who came second. Solon named two young men of Argos, the brothers Cleobis and Biton.

They were strong young men, both winners of athletic prizes. On the day of the festival of Hera, their mother had to be taken to the goddess's temple by ox cart (later writers say she was Hera's priestess). The oxen had not come back from the fields in time. So the brothers put themselves under the yoke and pulled the cart, with their mother on it, about forty-five stades, some eight kilometers, all the way to the temple.

The crowd at the festival praised them, the men for their strength and the women for the mother who had such sons. Overjoyed, the mother stood before the statue of Hera and prayed that the goddess would give her sons the best thing that can happen to a human being. After the sacrifice and the feast, the young men lay down to sleep in the temple and never woke up.

The Argives, Herodotus says, made statues of them and dedicated them at Delphi as men who had been the best of men.
lesson: Devotion to our parents is a form of greatness that ordinary people recognize at once. A good life is measured by its love and honor, not its wealth.
people: Cleobis, Biton, their mother (Cydippe in later sources), Solon, Croesus
caveat: Herodotus presents the tale as told by Solon; it is a legend, and the conversation between Solon and Croesus is chronologically doubtful.
